title: Honor the book (Avot 4:6)
hookLine: Yose: whoever honors the Torah is honored
tomorrow: can anyone judge alone? Avot says only One can.
last: NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.

cards: In some Jewish homes, if a siddur or a Bible hits the floor, someone picks it up and kisses it before putting it back.
Worn-out holy books aren't tossed in the recycling; traditionally they're buried, or set aside in a genizah.
Rabbi Yose says why it matters: whoever honors the Torah is honored by people, and whoever disgraces the Torah is disgraced by people.

teach.b: Yose doesn't say honor the book and you'll be rewarded later. He says people see it, and it changes how they see you. The way you treat what you hold sacred is public, even when you think it isn't.
A kiss on a dropped book is small. So is a hello said first, or a mouth kept shut in a group chat. That's the whole fortnight, really.
Deep roots: the deeds below ground. Essentials first: the poor mother's birds before the clever math. One mitzvah brings another.
Everyone has an hour. Very, very humble. Learn to do.
Not a crown, not a spade.

teach.h: IN THE HANDS, NOT THE HEAD.
teach.b: Each is a way of honoring the book: carrying it in your hands, not just your head. And the line runs the other way too: disgrace the Torah, and people see that as well.
Honor isn't only a private feeling; it's something your hands do.

how: Jews treat sacred books with care: some kiss a siddur that has fallen, and worn-out holy books are traditionally buried or stored in a genizah rather than thrown away.

o: keep books closed so they stay perfect
read only the books your teachers approve
treat sacred books with care, and honor returns

practice: Find a book near you that you value, sacred or not. Hold it in both hands, feel its weight and its cover, then set it down gently where it belongs. Let the rest of the sit be quiet, with it beside you.
